The yolk-dependent embryos develop entirely within the oviduct, drawing upon maternal provisions until the moment of parturition. Unlike many urodeles that undergo a prolonged aquatic tadpole phase, these offspring are born as miniature terrestrial juveniles, already possessing the fully resorbed gills and keratinised skin characteristic of their post-metamorphic condition. This direct developmental strategy, known as larviparity, results in relatively large neonates that are immediately capable of foraging on small invertebrates in the leaf litter. The body proportions at birth—a robust trunk and relatively short limbs—suggest a fossorial or cryptozoic lifestyle, which is typical of the genus. This pattern aligns with the broader ecological syndrome observed in many terrestrial salamanders occupying resource-limited Mediterranean environments. Comparisons with congeneric species, such as Lyciasalamandra billae and Lyciasalamandra helverseni, suggest that L. luschani occupies an intermediate position on the body-size continuum within the genus. This appears to be a relatively long-lived salamander for its body size, reflecting a life-history strategy centred on iteroparity and delayed senescence. The annual adult survival rate is high, as is typical for terrestrial urodeles that invest heavily in each reproductive event. The lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] is comparable to that of other lyciasalamandrines from the eastern Mediterranean, which also exhibit extended reproductive windows and low rates of extrinsic mortality. The combination of a late age at first reproduction, modest annual fecundity, and a decadal lifespan positions Lyciasalamandra luschani as an archetypal slow-living amphibian, adapted to the stable but resource-limited conditions of its subterranean refugia.
